9.2 Linear SVM in the Non-Separable Case: Slack Variables

9.2 Linear SVM in the Non-Separable Case: Slack Variables If the classes are not linearly separable, a zero training error is impossible and the hard-margin problem is infeasible. We therefore introduce slack variables \(\{\xi_i\}_{i=1}^{n}\) and relax the margin constraints to \[ y_i igl(x_i^T eta +  eta_0 igr) \ge 1-\xi_i,\qquad \xi_i\ge 0. \] Figure 9.3: Slack variables in the linearly non-separable case The value of \(\xi_i\) has a direct geometric reading: \(\xi_i=0\): the point is on the correct side and outside or on the margin. \(0<\xi_i\le 1\): the point is on the correct side but inside the margin. \(\xi_i>1\): the point is on the wrong side of the separating hyperplane. The soft-margin problem is \[ \operatorname{minimize}_{ eta,\, eta_0,\,\xi}\quad  rac12\| eta\|^2 + C\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_i \] \[ 	ext{subject to }\quad y_i igl(x_i^T eta+ eta_0 igr)\ge 1-\xi_i,\qquad \xi_i\ge 0,\qquad i=1,\ldots,n. \] The objective trades a large margin \(2/\| eta\|\) against the total slack \(\sum_i\xi_i\). The tuning parameter \(C>0\) is the cost of slack. A large \(C\) penalizes violations heavily and recovers the hard-margin problem as \(C	o\infty\). A small \(C\) tolerates more violations in exchange for a wider margin. In practice \(C\) is chosen by cross-validation. In these notes the parameter is \(C\). In e1071::svm() the same quantity is called cost. Solving the SVM with Slack Variables The Lagrangian of the primal is \[ egin{align*} \mathcal{L}( eta, eta_0,\xi,\alpha,\gamma) &=  rac12\| eta\|^2 + C\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_i - \sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i igl\{y_i(x_i^T eta+ eta_0)-(1-\xi_i) igr\} - \sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_i\xi_i, \end{align*}\] with \(\alpha_i\ge 0\) and \(\gamma_i\ge 0\). Stationarity yields \[ egin{align*} 
abla_{ eta}\mathcal{L}=0 &\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad  eta = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i y_i x_i,\ 
abla_{ eta_0}\mathcal{L}=0 &\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad \sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i y_i = 0,\ 
abla_{\xi_i}\mathcal{L}=0 &\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad C-\alpha_i-\gamma_i=0. \end{align*}\] The last identity, together with \(\gamma_i\ge 0\), forces \(0\le\alpha_i\le C\). Substituting back produces the soft-margin dual: \[ \max_{\alpha}\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i -  rac12\sum_{i,j=1}^{n} y_i y_j\alpha_i\alpha_j\,\langle x_i,x_jangle \] \[ 	ext{subject to }\quad 0\le\alpha_i\le C,\qquad i=1,\ldots,n, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i y_i=0. \] The inner product \(\langle x_i,x_jangle\) is just \(x_i^T x_j\). As before, \[ \hat eta = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat\alpha_i y_i x_i. \] The KKT complementary slackness conditions are \[ egin{align*} \alpha_i igl\{y_i(x_i^T eta+ eta_0)-(1-\xi_i) igr\}&=0,\ \gamma_i\xi_i&=0,\ y_i(x_i^T eta+ eta_0)-(1-\xi_i)&\ge 0. \end{align*}\] They partition the training points into three groups: \(\alpha_i=0\) (hence \(\xi_i=0\)): points strictly beyond the margin. They do not affect \(\hat eta\). \(0<\alpha_i<C\) (hence \(\xi_i=0\)): points on the margin. These are the free support vectors and are the ones used to recover \(\hat eta_0\). \(\alpha_i=C\): points inside the margin or on the wrong side, with \(\xi_i=1-y_i(x_i^T eta+ eta_0)\ge 0\). To compute \(\hat eta_0\), use any free support vector (\(0<\hat\alpha_i<C\)), for which \(y_i(x_i^T\hat eta+\hat eta_0)=1\). Averaging over all such points is more stable numerically. Do not use the hard-margin midpoint formula here: with slack, the closest points from each class may be inside the margin or misclassified. The two panels below use the same data with \(C=1000\) (left) and \(C=0.1\) (right). The plotted intercept is the solver intercept -svm.fit$rho, not the midpoint formula. A large \(C\) puts more weight on avoiding slack than on widening the margin. A small \(C\) does the reverse and is influenced more by points far from the boundary. In estimation language: large \(C\) is closer to empirical 0-1 risk; small \(C\) is more regularization. The same soft-margin program can be used on separable data as well: we may deliberately allow a few points to cross a margin line if that substantially increases the margin. The parameter \(C\) controls that trade-off.

9.3 Nonlinear SVM: The Kernel Trick In a linear SVM the decision boundaries are hyperplanes in the original input space. In many problems that is not flexible enough. ## Setting default kernel parameters Figure 9.4: A linear SVM on a nonlinear problem (ESL mixture data) To obtain nonlinear boundaries we enlarge the feature space with a map \[ \Phi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{F},\qquad \Phi(x)=\bigl(\phi_1(x),\phi_2(x),\ldots\bigr), \] where \(\mathcal{F}\) may be finite- or infinite-dimensional, and then run a linear SVM in \(\mathcal{F}\). A linear function of \(\Phi(x)\) is typically a nonlinear function of the original \(x\). The decision function becomes \[ f(x)=\bigl\langle\Phi(x),\beta\bigr\rangle=\Phi(x)^T\beta. \] Kernel trick Do not compute \(\Phi(x)\) explicitly. The dual SVM depends on the data only through inner products, and \[ K(x,z)=\bigl\langle\Phi(x),\Phi(z)\bigr\rangle \] can often be evaluated directly in the original space. Naive Approach If \(\Phi\) were known, we could form \(\Phi(x_i)\) for each \(i\) and solve \[ \max_{\alpha} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i - \frac12\sum_{i,j=1}^{n} y_i y_j\alpha_i\alpha_j \underbrace{\bigl\langle\Phi(x_i),\Phi(x_j)\bigr\rangle}_{=K(x_i,x_j)} \] \[ \text{subject to }\quad 0\le\alpha_i\le C,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i y_i=0. \] The kernel trick lets us evaluate \(K(x_i,x_j)\) without ever forming \(\Phi(x_i)\). A simple example: the homogeneous quadratic kernel \(K(x,z)=(x^T z)^2\) with \(x,z\in\mathbb{R}^p\). Let \(\Phi(x)\) collect all monomials \(x_k x_{\ell}\) for \(1\le k,\ell\le p\). Then \[\begin{align*} K(x,z) &= \Bigl(\sum_{k=1}^{p} x_k z_k\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{\ell=1}^{p} x_{\ell} z_{\ell}\Bigr)\\ &= \sum_{k=1}^{p}\sum_{\ell=1}^{p} (x_k x_{\ell})(z_k z_{\ell})\\ &= \bigl\langle\Phi(x),\Phi(z)\bigr\rangle. \end{align*}\] The kernel trick is useful for two reasons. The dual depends on the training data only through the pairwise values \(K(x_i,x_j)\). We never have to form \(\Phi(x_i)\). The fitted decision function can be written in terms of those same kernel evaluations, \[ f(x)=\beta_0+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i y_i K(x,x_i) \] (or an equivalent expansion, depending on how \(\alpha\) is coded). In other words, \(\hat f\) lives in the span of \(\{K(\cdot,x_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}\). Remark. A sufficient condition is that the kernel matrix \(\bigl(K(x_i,x_j)\bigr)\) be positive semidefinite for every finite sample. Then \(K\) is an inner product \(\langle\Phi(x),\Phi(z)\rangle\) for some feature map \(\Phi\) (Mercer’s theorem). We will use that fact and will not develop the RKHS formalism further here. #### Computational Advantage {-} Evaluating \(K(x,z)=(x^T z)^2\) costs \(\mathcal{O}(p)\) operations. Forming \(\Phi(x)\) and \(\Phi(z)\) and then taking an inner product costs \(\mathcal{O}(p^2)\). That is why we derived the dual: the primal is written in terms of \(\beta\in\mathcal{F}\), which we cannot even store when \(\mathcal{F}\) is infinite-dimensional, whereas the dual is written entirely in terms of \(K(x_i,x_j)\). Common kernels Degree-\(d\) polynomial: \[ K(x,z)=(1+x^T z)^d \] Radial basis (Gaussian): \[ K(x,z)=\exp\bigl(-\|x-z\|^2/c\bigr) \] Sigmoid (listed for completeness; do not use it by default): \[ K(x,z)=\tanh(\gamma x^T z + r) \] Remark. Not every function \(K\) is a valid kernel. If the kernel matrix fails to be positive semidefinite, the dual need not be convex and there may be no feature map \(\Phi\). The sigmoid kernel is a historical choice from early neural-network comparisons. It is not always positive semidefinite; prefer a polynomial or radial kernel unless you have a specific reason not to. Remark on Convexity Is the dual still convex after we replace \(x_i^T x_j\) by \(K(x_i,x_j)\)? The quadratic term is \[ \sum_{i,j=1}^{n} y_i y_j\alpha_i\alpha_j K(x_i,x_j) = \alpha^T \operatorname{diag}(y)\,K\,\operatorname{diag}(y)\,\alpha. \] This is a convex function of \(\alpha\) whenever \(K\) is positive semidefinite, which is the same condition that lets us treat \(K(x,z)\) as an inner product \(\langle\Phi(x),\Phi(z)\rangle\).

9.4 SVM as a Penalization Method The soft-margin constraint \(y_i f(x_i)\ge 1-\xi_i\) with \(\xi_i\ge 0\) is equivalent to \(\xi_i\ge \bigl(1-y_i f(x_i)\bigr)_+\). Substituting the smallest feasible slacks into the primal objective gives \[ \operatorname{minimize}_{f}\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(1-y_i f(x_i)\bigr)_+ + \lambda\|\beta\|^2, \] where \(\lambda=1/C\) and \(f(x)=x^T\beta+\beta_0\). This is a loss + penalty problem. The loss is the hinge loss \[ L(y,f(x))=\bigl(1-yf(x)\bigr)_+ = \max\bigl(0,\ 1-yf(x)\bigr). \] Hinge loss is not differentiable at \(yf(x)=1\), so we cannot use ordinary gradient descent without modification (a subgradient does exist). Other convex surrogate losses used for classification include: Logistic loss: \[ L(y,f(x))=\log\bigl(1+e^{-yf(x)}\bigr) \] Modified Huber loss: \[ L(y,f(x))= \begin{cases} \bigl(1-yf(x)\bigr)^2, & yf(x)\ge -1,\\ -4yf(x), & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \] Zero-one loss is the target, but it is discontinuous and nonconvex. Hinge, logistic, and modified Huber are convex surrogates and are much easier to optimize. Logistic and modified Huber are differentiable, so gradient methods apply directly and can be attractive when \(n\) is large. The contrast with the previous chapter is useful here. Logistic loss is (up to constants) the negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli model, so we can map \(\hat f\) to \(\widehat{P}(Y=1\mid X=x)\) by the logistic transform. Hinge loss only cares that \(yf(x)\) be at least \(1\); once a point is beyond the margin it costs nothing further. That is why an SVM is a classifier and not, by itself, a probability model. A nonlinear SVM with hinge loss solves \[ \min_{f\in\mathcal{H}_K} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(1-y_i f(x_i)\bigr)_+ + \lambda\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_K}^2, \] where \(\mathcal{H}_K\) is the RKHS of the kernel \(K\). By the representer theorem the solution has the form \[ \hat f(x)=\alpha_0+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i K(x,x_i). \] The problem reduces to an optimization over \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} L\bigl(y_i,\ K_i^T\alpha\bigr) + \lambda\,\alpha^T K\alpha, \] where \(K\) is the \(n\times n\) kernel matrix and \(K_i\) is its \(i\)th column. If \(L\) is differentiable this is an unconstrained smooth problem. In this view a kernel SVM first builds \(n\) new predictors, each measuring similarity to one training point, and then fits a linear model in those predictors with an \(\ell_2\)-type penalty \(\alpha^T K\alpha\). Two restrictions of the classical SVM are worth questioning once we adopt the loss-plus-penalty view: The penalty on \(\alpha\) is a ridge (RKHS-norm) penalty. A lasso-type penalty on \(\alpha\) would produce a sparser expansion, using fewer kernel centers. The kernel is required to be positive semidefinite. Many useful similarity functions are not. Relaxing either condition takes us outside the textbook definition of an SVM, but the resulting kernel machines are often useful supervised learning methods. When an SVM is the wrong tool An SVM is a strong binary classifier. It is not a default replacement for logistic regression or DA. It does not produce \(\widehat{P}(Y=1\mid X)\) without an extra calibration step (Platt scaling and relatives). If the scientific target is a probability, start with logistic regression. Multiclass problems are handled by one-versus-one or one-versus-rest reductions. That works, but it is bolted on; there is no single native multiclass hinge in the same way that multinomial logistic regression is native. When \(n\) is large or \(p\) is huge and sparsity in the original features is the point, \(\ell_1\)-penalized logistic regression is often the simpler statistical and computational story. The SVM sparsity is in the \(\alpha_i\) (support vectors), not in the coordinates of \(x\). A radial kernel with a poorly chosen width will look excellent on the training plot and fail on a new draw. Scale the features, and treat \(C\) and the kernel width as tuning parameters chosen by prediction error, not by how pretty the decision regions are. Use an SVM when you want a flexible decision boundary and you are willing to treat \(f(x)\) as a score rather than a probability. Use logistic regression or DA when the probability model, or the linear structure in \(x\), is the object of interest.

9.5 SVM Examples in R This section is an illustration of the methods discussed in this week’s lectures. The code shows how the objects from the notes, e.g., \(\beta\), \(C\), support vectors, kernels appear in a fitted SVM. The Python version of the example can be found here: Python Code for SVM .  The calculations use e1071::svm(). Its argument cost is the \(C\) of the notes. We keep scale = FALSE when we want coefficients and plots in the original units of \(X\). In applications one would usually scale the features. Three comparisons: a hard margin versus a soft margin (what \(C\) does); a linear SVM versus logistic regression on the same points (who influences the fit); a linear kernel versus a radial kernel, with the Bayes boundary as a reference. Linear Separable Case: Maximal Margin Classifier We start with a small maximal-margin example (adapted from an ISLR exercise). X1 X2 Y 3 4 red 2 2 red 4 4 red 1 4 red 2 1 blue 4 3 blue 4 1 blue A scatterplot of the data: The linear separating hyperplane has the form \[ \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 = 0. \] We compute it from a hard-margin SVM fit in e1071 by taking a very large cost: library(e1071) # large C approximates a hard margin svm.toy <- svm(Y ~ ., data = toy.data, kernel = "linear", cost = 1e+05, scale = FALSE) The coefficients of the separating line are b <- t(svm.toy$coefs) %*% svm.toy$SV c <- -svm.toy$rho b ## X1 X2 ## [1,] -1.999846 1.999693 c ## [1] 1.00041 so the optimal separating hyperplane is \[ 1 - 2X_1 + 2X_2 = 0. \] slope <- -b[1]/b[2] b0 <- -c/b[2] slope ## [1] 1.000077 b0 ## [1] -0.5002816 The decision boundary is the line \[ X_2 = X_1 - 0.5, \] and the maximal-margin classifier can be written \[ f(X) = X_2 - X_1 + 0.5. \] A new point \(x^*\) is assigned to the red class if \(f(x^*)>0\) and to the blue class otherwise. The margin width is \(2/\|\beta\|\): margin <- 2/sqrt(sum(b^2)) margin ## [1] 0.7071882 The solid line is the optimal separating hyperplane; the dotted lines are the margins. The fit used scale = FALSE and a large cost so that this is, for practical purposes, the hard-margin solution in the original coordinates. In e1071, svm.toy$index identifies the support vectors and svm.toy$rho is the intercept used in the plot (not the hard-margin midpoint formula). svm.toy$index ## [1] 2 3 6 svm.toy$nSV ## [1] 2 1 Those indices are the support vectors: the active points on the two dotted lines. For a hard-margin fit, \(y_i f(x_i)\ge 1\) at every training point, with equality only on this subset. The printed margin \(2/\|\beta\|\) is the width between the dotted lines. Non-Separable Data and the Role of \(C\) Add a red point at \((X_1,X_2)=(3,1)\). The data are no longer linearly separable. toy.data.2 <- data.frame(X1 = c(3, 2, 4, 1, 2, 4, 4, 3), X2 = c(4, 2, 4, 4, 1, 3, 1, 1), Y = as.factor(c("red", "red", "red", "red", "blue", "blue", "blue", "red"))) A finite cost is now required. Large \(C\) tries to avoid slack (narrower margin, fewer violations). Small \(C\) allows more violations and a wider margin. The plotted intercept is again -fit$rho. plot_linear_svm <- function(fit, data, main) { b <- as.numeric(t(fit$coefs) %*% fit$SV) b0 <- -fit$rho x <- data[, c("X1", "X2")] plot(x, col = ifelse(data$Y == "blue", "blue", "red"), xlim = c(0, 5), ylim = c(0, 5), pch = 19, xlab = "X1", ylab = "X2", main = main) abline(a = -b0/b[2], b = -b[1]/b[2], lwd = 2) points(x[fit$index, ], col = "black", cex = 2.4) abline(a = (-b0 - 1)/b[2], b = -b[1]/b[2], lty = 3) abline(a = (-b0 + 1)/b[2], b = -b[1]/b[2], lty = 3) } svm.hiC <- svm(Y ~ ., data = toy.data.2, kernel = "linear", cost = 10, scale = FALSE) svm.loC <- svm(Y ~ ., data = toy.data.2, kernel = "linear", cost = 0.5, scale = FALSE) par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot_linear_svm(svm.hiC, toy.data.2, main = paste0("C = 10, nSV = ", sum(svm.hiC$nSV))) plot_linear_svm(svm.loC, toy.data.2, main = paste0("C = 0.5, nSV = ", sum(svm.loC$nSV))) The extra red point is expensive when \(C=10\): the boundary moves toward it and the margin shrinks. When \(C=0.5\) that point is tolerated as slack, more points become support vectors, and the margin widens. This is an estimation statement, not just a geometric one. Large \(C\) is closer to empirical 0-1 risk (fit the training labels, even the noisy ones). Small \(C\) is more regularization (a smaller \(\|\beta\|\), a wider margin, more slack). The left panel weaves toward the extra point; the right panel is willing to ignore it. Linear SVM versus Logistic Regression On the same eight points, fit a linear logistic regression. Both methods give a line; they do not use the data in the same way. toy.data.2$y01 <- as.numeric(toy.data.2$Y == "red") glm.toy <- glm(y01 ~ X1 + X2, data = toy.data.2, family = binomial) b.svm <- as.numeric(t(svm.hiC$coefs) %*% svm.hiC$SV) b0.svm <- -svm.hiC$rho b.glm <- coef(glm.toy) plot(toy.data.2$X1, toy.data.2$X2, col = ifelse(toy.data.2$Y == "blue", "blue", "red"), pch = 19, xlim = c(0, 5), ylim = c(0, 5), xlab = "X1", ylab = "X2", main = "Linear SVM (C = 10) vs logistic") points(toy.data.2[svm.hiC$index, c("X1", "X2")], cex = 2.4) abline(a = -b0.svm/b.svm[2], b = -b.svm[1]/b.svm[2], lwd = 2) abline(a = -b.glm[1]/b.glm[3], b = -b.glm[2]/b.glm[3], col = "darkorange", lwd = 2, lty = 2) legend("bottomright", c("SVM", "Logistic", "SVM support vectors"), col = c("black", "darkorange", "black"), lty = c(1, 2, NA), pch = c(NA, NA, 1), lwd = 2, bty = "n") Logistic regression is a likelihood for \(P(Y=1\mid X)\). Every point contributes to the score equations. The SVM with hinge loss ignores points that already lie beyond the margin; only the support vectors (circled) determine the black line. The two boundaries need not agree, even when both are linear. Logistic regression still produces \(\widehat{P}(Y=1\mid X)\); the SVM does not. Nonlinear SVM: Linear Kernel, Radial Kernel, Bayes Rule The mixture data from ESL are not linearly separable in a way that matches the Bayes boundary (the red dashed \(P(Y=1\mid X)=1/2\) contour). A linear SVM can only draw a line. A radial kernel can bend. library(mda) data(ESL.mixture) px1 <- ESL.mixture$px1 px2 <- ESL.mixture$px2 mix <- data.frame(X1 = ESL.mixture$x[, 1], X2 = ESL.mixture$x[, 2], y = factor(ESL.mixture$y)) prob <- ESL.mixture$prob xgrid <- expand.grid(X1 = px1, X2 = px2) svm.lin <- svm(y ~ ., data = mix, kernel = "linear", cost = 10, scale = FALSE) svm.rad <- svm(y ~ ., data = mix, kernel = "radial", cost = 5, scale = FALSE) plot_mixture <- function(fit, main) { dec <- predict(fit, xgrid, decision.values = TRUE) z <- attributes(dec)$decision yhat <- predict(fit, xgrid) plot(xgrid, col = ifelse(yhat == levels(mix$y)[2], "bisque", "cadetblue1"), pch = 20, cex = 0.2, xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2", main = main) points(mix$X1, mix$X2, col = ifelse(mix$y == 1, "darkorange", "deepskyblue"), pch = 19) contour(px1, px2, matrix(z, length(px1), length(px2)), levels = 0, add = TRUE, lwd = 2) contour(px1, px2, matrix(prob, length(px1), length(px2)), levels = 0.5, add = TRUE, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2) } par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot_mixture(svm.lin, "Linear kernel, C = 10") plot_mixture(svm.rad, "Radial kernel, C = 5") The red dashed curve is the Bayes boundary. The linear kernel cannot track it. The radial kernel can, but only for a reasonable \(C\) (and kernel width). That is the point of this figure: the kernel changes the class of boundaries, \(C\) changes how hard we fit within that class. Tuning \(C\) by Cross-Validation \(C\) is a regularization parameter. We choose it by cross-validation, not by looking at the training plot. e1071::tune() does a grid search and returns the CV error. The radial kernel also has a width parameter gamma (large gamma is a narrow kernel). set.seed(1) tune.lin <- tune(svm, y ~ ., data = mix, kernel = "linear", scale = FALSE, ranges = list(cost = 2^seq(-3, 5, by = 1))) tune.lin$best.parameters ## cost ## 2 0.25 plot(tune.lin) set.seed(1) tune.rad <- tune(svm, y ~ ., data = mix, kernel = "radial", scale = FALSE, ranges = list(cost = c(0.5, 1, 5, 10), gamma = c(0.5, 1, 2))) tune.rad$best.parameters ## cost gamma ## 7 5 1 tune.rad$best.performance ## [1] 0.165 Read the linear plot as you would a ridge CV curve: very small \(C\) underfits (wide margin, too much slack), very large \(C\) starts to overfit the training labels. The “best” \(C\) is the one with the smallest estimated prediction error, not the prettiest training margin. If you already use caret in the course, the same idea can be written as train(..., method = "svmRadial"), where C is \(C\) and sigma is the radial width. What matters is the CV curve, not the wrapper.
